You are studying about world ecological problems・You are going to read the
following article to understand what has happened with palm oil.
Palm
oil
is used as an ingredient
in nearly half the products you
might buy from a supermarket.
Not long ago, however, palm oil had a bad
reputation.
Many tropical forests have been burned down to make space to
grow oil palm trees, releasing carbon dioxide into the air and damaging the
environment.
Consequently, environmentalists began
to consider palm
oil
production unethical and even encouraged people not to buy products made
from it・Recently, however, recognizing the importance of palm oil for farmers
around the world, they are instead focusing on helping them produce
it in a
more sustainable wav.
The popularity of palm oil is due to its many properties and uses.
It is
almost solid
at room temperature, for example, so
it
is a useful ingredient
for margarine, mayonnaise, and other semi-solid spread foods.
It also helps
preserve food by slowing down the effects of spoiling.
For producers, palm oil
is easier to grow than crops such as soybeans and coconut oil, and it requires
fewer chemicals to protect the plants from insects.
Farmers produced more than 70 million tons of palm
oil in 2018, with
more than 60 million tons coming from lndonesia and Malaysia alone.
Demand
has grown steadily from the early 1990s, when thousands of acres of forests
were burned
to make space for new palm
oil plantations, particularly in
Indonesia.
By 2006, Indonesia had become the world's largest producer, and
currently manufactures twice as much palm oil as Malaysia.
As the industry
grew,
it contributed significantly to global deforestation.
In response,
a non-
profit group called the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm
Oil (RSPO), was set
up in 2004 to certify palm oil products that are grown from ethical sources.
It seeks to reduce the negative effects on the environment and communities.
Their criteria for producers who want to be certified include minimal use of
fire to clear land, fair treatment of workers, and proper consultation with local
communities about land development.
The RSPO reports that an increasing
－⑤－26－

number of producers are committed to such sustainable practices.
Although
certification
is not a legal requirement, shoppers who want to support
sustainable practices can now look for the RSPO symbol on palm-oil products.
Meanwhile, scientists
at an environmental research organization,
SMARTRI, are being paid
to advise the
oil palm industry on sustainable
practices.
Scientists at SMARTRI believe that because palm oil is such an
important crop, such partnerships are vital. They point out that the lndonesian
government's new laws to stop unethical practices of the past have not been
successful because some forests and communities are still being destroyed by
unethical companies.
Critics who distrust the industry, however, suggest that
the scientists' research is not independent.
They suspect that the companies'
intentions are to pay the scientists to improve the industry's reputation while
not changing their unethical practices.
Others believe that any efforts to make
the production of this important colnmodity more sustainable are worthwhile.
